paragraphs: AtomWorld evaluates whether language models can modify atomic structures, an important part of materials research that involves more than recalling scientific facts. Existing materials benchmarks emphasize knowledge or perception, leaving structure construction and manipulation comparatively untested. The paper brings this spatial work into an evaluation where the correctness of modifications can be checked.

The benchmark organizes ten basic actions into four commonly used modelling categories. This structure lets the authors examine performance across different operations and levels of complexity. Its emphasis on verifiable modifications matters because a model's ability to discuss a material does not establish that it can correctly change the arrangement of its atoms.

Gemini 2.5 Pro generally performs best in the reported evaluation, but success drops substantially as modelling becomes more complex. Rotation is especially difficult, with success rates below 12%. These findings support using current models as supervised copilots for structure modelling. AtomWorld also provides a setting for developing and evaluating future models that better understand atomic geometry.
icml-2026-atomworld-a-benchmark-for-eval.tldr: AtomWorld tests language models on atomic structure modifications and finds substantial weaknesses in complex spatial operations.

paragraphs: Strategic classification studies what happens when people change their features to obtain a more favorable decision from a classifier. Many existing approaches assume that these changes follow strictly rational calculations. This paper formalizes a setting in which psychological biases shape those responses, making the behavior anticipated by the model different from fully rational optimization.

The proposed Prospect-Guided Strategic Framework, or Pro-SF, uses prospect theory to describe this interaction. It incorporates three mechanisms: people can evaluate benefits and costs asymmetrically, judge outcomes relative to different subjective reference points, and distort probabilities. These mechanisms enter the interaction between the decision-maker and responding agents, allowing learning to account for behavior that conventional rational-response models omit.

Experiments use both synthetic and real-world datasets to evaluate the framework. The stated contribution is a behaviorally grounded approach to modelling strategic responses and learning under them. Its practical significance is that deployment planning can explicitly include psychological influences on feature manipulation, rather than depending entirely on an idealized account of how people respond.
icml-2026-beyond-rational-illusion-behav.tldr: Pro-SF incorporates prospect-theory mechanisms into strategic classification to account for psychologically biased responses to classifiers.

paragraphs: DC-LA addresses sampling from a distribution defined by a smooth data-fitting term and a potentially nonsmooth regularizer. The regularizer must be expressible as one convex function minus another. This structure accommodates a broader sampling problem than one restricted to a convex overall objective, while giving the algorithm specific mathematical components to work with.

The method smooths the two convex components separately using Moreau envelopes. It then moves the concave contribution into the data-fitting term and applies a corresponding proximal Langevin algorithm. The distinction matters: the procedure uses the regularizer's decomposition to construct a tractable sampling method instead of treating its nonsmooth, nonconvex behavior as an undifferentiated obstacle.

Under the stated distant-dissipativity assumption on V, the authors establish convergence toward the target distribution in q-Wasserstein distance for every positive integer q, allowing for discretization and smoothing errors. Synthetic experiments show accurate sampled distributions. A computed tomography application provides qualitatively reasonable uncertainty estimates, supporting the method's practical relevance without claiming exact sampling or quantitatively validated uncertainty in that application.
icml-2026-dc-la-difference-of-convex-lan.tldr: DC-LA uses a difference-of-convex decomposition to sample nonsmooth distributions with conditional convergence guarantees and controlled approximation errors.

paragraphs: The paper asks why frozen representations learned without labels can support classification with very few labeled examples. Its central quantity, directional CDNV, measures variability along the directions that separate classes. The key idea is that variation matters differently depending on its direction: substantial overall variation can coexist with little variation along the axes used for classification.

The authors prove multiclass generalization bounds whose leading term is directional CDNV. Additional terms account for having only a finite number of labeled examples, separating intrinsic variability from errors in estimating class centers. They also show that, for independent balanced labelings, small directional CDNV across tasks forces their decision axes to be nearly orthogonal, helping explain low interference between tasks.

Across self-supervised objectives, directional CDNV decreases during pretraining even when its classical counterpart remains large. The bounds closely follow observed classification error at practical label counts. Synthetic multitask experiments also show nearly orthogonal decision axes. Together, these findings connect useful transfer to a specific geometry of class separation, with the multitask theoretical claim depending on the stated labeling assumptions.
icml-2026-directional-neural-collapse-ex.tldr: Low representation variability along class-separating directions helps explain few-shot transfer and, under stated labeling assumptions, reduced interference across tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether predictions about state transitions can reduce the samples needed to solve an infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision process. The setting provides a generative model for obtaining samples, plus black-box predictions of the transition matrix. The challenge is that the algorithm does not know how accurate those predictions are.

The authors first establish a worst-case barrier. With unknown prediction accuracy, no sampling policy can universally improve on the established minimax sample-complexity scaling for finding an approximately optimal policy without predictions. This prevents interpreting predictive advice as an automatic reduction in the information that must be collected.

They then develop a minimax-optimization algorithm whose sample bound adapts to prediction error without requiring that error as an input. Its bound uniformly improves on the previous convex-optimization-based result and, in some cases, improves on the standard minimax benchmark. These conclusions are compatible: predictions cannot guarantee a better worst case across all settings, yet can produce stronger guarantees in favorable cases. The contribution combines that opportunity with an explicit account of its worst-case limit.
icml-2026-efficiently-solving-discounted.tldr: Transition predictions can improve discounted-MDP sample efficiency in favorable cases without known prediction accuracy, despite a worst-case impossibility bound.

paragraphs: Activation functions such as Swish and GELU can be expensive on edge hardware because their computations involve operations such as exponentiation and division. When those operations lack fast hardware support, the cost can restrict the use of otherwise accurate models. The paper targets this overhead by replacing activation computations after training.

FFCC is a compiler that takes activation functions expressed through basic floating-point operators and derives efficient approximations. It uses floating-point reinterpretation and transformation rules to produce short instruction sequences. The resulting functions are designed to remain fast without specialized hardware paths while being accurate enough to substitute into an already trained model.

Experiments report order-of-magnitude activation-level speedups over accurate baselines on Arm M7, Aarch64, and Intel platforms. A ConvNeXt example shows that these local savings can translate into faster overall inference without significant accuracy loss. The distinction between activation-level and end-to-end results matters: the large reported speedups concern the activation computations, while the model example demonstrates their practical contribution to total inference time.
icml-2026-faster-activation-functions-at.tldr: FFCC compiles fast activation approximations that can replace trained-model activations and reduce inference time without significant accuracy loss in the reported example.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow-based policies can express complex continuous actions, but their action probabilities are not directly available. That complicates maximum-entropy reinforcement learning, which seeks strong returns while retaining policy randomness. FLAC addresses this difficulty by controlling the energy of the generative process instead of explicitly estimating action densities.

The method formulates policy optimization as a Generalized Schrödinger Bridge problem relative to a high-entropy reference process. Staying close to that reference encourages stochastic behavior while the policy improves its return. The kinetic energy of the velocity field provides a proxy for departure from the reference: reducing energy along the generative paths bounds the deviation of the resulting action distribution.

From this formulation, the authors derive energy-regularized policy iteration and a practical off-policy algorithm. A Lagrangian dual mechanism automatically adjusts the energy regulation. On high-dimensional benchmarks, FLAC performs better than or comparably to strong baselines while avoiding explicit density estimation. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical route to entropy-oriented policy learning and an implementable algorithm for expressive generative policies.
icml-2026-flac-maximum-entropy-rl-via-ki.tldr: FLAC regulates generative policies through kinetic energy, enabling maximum-entropy reinforcement learning without explicit action-density estimation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses generalization from limited data in embodied intelligence. Its diagnosis is that predicting absolute coordinates entangles the underlying geometry of a task with particular execution speeds and motion styles. The Generalized Action Manifold framework, or GAM, separates these factors so that learned actions can represent a broader set of valid executions.

GAM introduces two complementary forms of invariance. An Arc-Length Parameterizer separates the shape of a spatial path from its timing, supporting robustness to speed changes. A Schema-Affine-Factorization mechanism maps trajectories into canonical world lines in a Lie-algebraic tangent space. This separates invariant topological schemas from affine changes, providing a structured representation for spatial variation.

The authors integrate these components into a vision-language-action architecture, using sparse training data to construct a continuous manifold of valid actions. Their experiments report stronger transfer and robustness than geometry-agnostic baselines. The stated result supports the value of explicitly representing which aspects of an action remain stable and which may vary, rather than binding every demonstration to its original coordinates and timing.
icml-2026-general-covariant-action-model.tldr: GAM separates action geometry from timing and spatial transformations to improve transfer and robustness from limited embodied training data.

paragraphs: Learning representative patterns from time series is difficult when observations mix underlying dynamics with random noise. The paper addresses this ambiguity in early link failure detection, where measurements can arrive at irregular intervals. It also challenges a fixed set of pattern categories, because that restriction may fail to capture previously unseen variation.

The proposed clustering network represents latent state evolution through a neural ordinary differential equation. This produces a continuous trajectory rather than only a sequence of disconnected states. Enforcing temporal continuity helps separate smooth feature trends from stochastic fluctuations. Alongside this continuous-time model, an adaptive hierarchy determines the number of prototypes instead of requiring a rigid count in advance.

Validation on early link failure detection shows that the method extracts underlying physical prototypes from irregularly sampled data and enables robust detection. The two design choices address different sources of ambiguity: continuous dynamics organize how features evolve, while the adaptive hierarchy accommodates diversity in the patterns being learned. The reported findings support their combined use for recognizing failure-related behavior in this task.
icml-2026-hierarchical-ode-learning-cont.tldr: A hierarchical neural ODE learns continuous-time prototypes and their number adaptively to support early link failure detection.

paragraphs: Open-world object detection must recognize known categories while also identifying objects outside those categories. This paper argues that improving unknown-object recall alone leaves an important problem unresolved: a detector can still confuse known and unknown objects without exposing why. IPOW introduces an interpretable representation intended to improve both recognition and the explanation of predictions.

Its Concept Decomposition Model splits Faster R-CNN region features into discriminative, shared, and background concepts. Discriminative concepts help separate known classes. Shared and background concepts provide information that can transfer to unknown categories. This division gives the detector distinct representational components whose roles can be examined for both known and unknown predictions.

Using that decomposition, the authors identify confusion when unknown objects enter the discriminative feature space associated with known classes. They introduce Concept-Guided Rectification to address this overlap. Experiments report significantly improved unknown recall alongside reduced confusion. The contribution connects interpretability to a concrete correction mechanism: exposing the source of a mistaken classification helps guide how the detector should be adjusted.
icml-2026-knowing-the-unknown-interpreta.tldr: IPOW decomposes object features into interpretable concepts to improve unknown-object detection and reduce confusion with known classes.

paragraphs: LAST addresses how a vision-language-action model should connect semantic similarity with physical similarity between motions. The paper formulates this as a Gromov-Wasserstein alignment problem. Its central difficulty is a mismatch in geometry: vision-language representations are described as linear and isotropic, while robotic action occupies a non-Euclidean, direction-dependent space.

The proposed Lie-algebraic Action Space Tokenizer reconstructs the action representation in two stages. First, it maps trajectories into a fixed-length, physically additive representation through Lie-algebraic linearization. Second, it discretizes that representation hierarchically into schemas and whitened residuals. The first stage addresses global structure; the second adjusts local metric structure to align with an isotropic Euclidean geometry.

This reconstruction is intended to make relationships within the action space more compatible with relationships in vision-language embeddings. The paper states that resolving the mismatch enables better convergence and generalization in VLA models. Its main contribution is therefore an action tokenizer designed around the geometry of cross-modal alignment, giving semantic-to-motion learning a more consistent representation on which to operate.
icml-2026-last-bridging-vision-language-.tldr: LAST restructures robotic action representations to align their geometry with vision-language embeddings and improve VLA learning.

paragraphs: Light Forcing targets the attention cost of autoregressive video generation. The authors find that sparse-attention methods developed for bidirectional models lose quality when transferred to this setting. They attribute the problem to treating video chunks too independently and failing to retain useful information from earlier chunks.

The method combines two mechanisms. Chunk-Aware Growth estimates each chunk's contribution and assigns sparsity accordingly, progressively increasing sparsity while allowing the current chunk to draw on earlier information. Hierarchical Sparse Attention then selects context at both frame and block levels. This coarse-to-fine selection accommodates different attention patterns while retaining informative historical and nearby content.

Experiments report better quality and efficiency than existing sparse-attention approaches, including a VBench score of 84.5 and end-to-end speedups of 1.2–1.3 times. Combining Light Forcing with other efficiency methods produces larger speedups of 2.0–3.0 times across different GPUs. Those combined gains should be distinguished from the gains of sparse attention alone. The results support allocating attention according to the sequential dependencies of autoregressive video.
icml-2026-light-forcing-accelerating-aut.tldr: Light Forcing uses chunk-aware, hierarchical sparse attention to accelerate autoregressive video generation while preserving useful historical context.

paragraphs: NaviCache accelerates video diffusion by improving decisions about when computational blocks can be skipped. Offline calibration can be costly and sensitive to distribution changes. Existing approaches that avoid offline calibration instead rely on immediate approximations, which the paper argues are vulnerable to noise and fail to capture momentum in evolving diffusion features.

The method treats feature evolution as an inertial navigation problem. It tracks both the ratio between input and output changes and a latent drift in that ratio. A dedicated initial alignment phase establishes these estimates. Subsequent updates combine a time-dependent noise schedule with uncertainty-aware measurements, allowing the estimates to adapt as the diffusion process changes.

This tracking mechanism provides a theoretically grounded approach to block skipping with bounded error. Experiments on the HunyuanVideo, Wan, and Open-Sora series report more accurate judgments of skipping error and strong overall performance. The approach matters because a skip decision depends on how feature changes are evolving over time, not just on the latest observed difference; NaviCache explicitly models that temporal information.
icml-2026-navicache-test-time-self-calib.tldr: NaviCache tracks feature-change dynamics and uncertainty during video generation to make more accurate, error-bounded block-skipping decisions.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion language models can generate multiple tokens at once, but choosing positions solely by confidence overlooks their interactions. The paper argues that this creates a poor compromise: aggressive parallel generation loses quality, while cautious decoding approaches slow, token-by-token behavior. It proposes changing the unmasking schedule without modifying the underlying model.

The Dilated Unmasking Scheduler divides positions into spaced, non-adjacent groups and unmasks each group in parallel. Its scheduling criterion aims to minimize an upper bound on joint entropy gain at each denoising step. A block-size parameter controls the trade-off between network calls and output quality, making the degree of parallelism explicit without requiring a separate planner model.

Across mathematics, coding, knowledge, and instruction-following benchmarks, DUS outperforms confidence-based planners and recovers much of the quality lost with conventional parallel unmasking. Reported wall-clock speedups reach 5.8 times compared with token-by-token MDLM decoding. Dilated spacing also improves adaptive samplers when added as a post-filter. These findings show that the arrangement of simultaneously generated positions can materially affect decoding efficiency.
icml-2026-plan-for-speed-dilated-schedul.tldr: DUS unmasks spaced token groups in parallel, improving the quality-speed trade-off of masked diffusion decoding without changing the denoiser.

paragraphs: Generating hardware RTL from detailed specifications becomes difficult as both the documents and the resulting code grow. Important interface requirements can be buried among unrelated details, long outputs lose syntactic and semantic correctness, and debugging requires simulation and waveform analysis. ChipV-RTL addresses these connected problems at the scale of IP-level Verilog designs.

The framework uses multiple agents and the modular structure of hardware to divide a long-document, long-code task into smaller tasks. It partitions specifications hierarchically, plans work, generates code locally, and merges components while preserving interface consistency. Debugging uses abstract syntax trees to focus attention on relevant local code. Locality therefore guides generation, integration, and correction.

On the RealBench IP-level benchmark, ChipV-RTL achieves a 45.0% pass rate compared with the reported 21.6% comparison result, substantially outperforming existing models and agents. The result supports organizing the task around component-specific information while explicitly maintaining shared interfaces. It demonstrates improved success on a demanding generation benchmark, with the reported pass rate also making clear that complete functional success remains far from universal.
icml-2026-qimeng-chipv-rtl-exploiting-in.tldr: ChipV-RTL decomposes IP-level hardware generation into local, interface-consistent tasks and raises the reported benchmark pass rate to 45.0%.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can increase training variety when examples are scarce, but the added images may introduce misleading information. This paper identifies two forms of semantic infidelity: visual problems such as artifacts and unnatural blending, and mismatches between an augmented image and its assigned label. The latter can turn augmentation into a source of label noise.

SCalDA combines diffusion-enhanced augmentation with semantic calibration across images, labels, and features. Its components include precise guidance in the label domain, synthesis driven by semantics across all three domains, and semantics-aware metric learning. The design treats the generated appearance, its supervision, and its learned representation as linked parts of the same augmentation process.

Experiments across multiple datasets report consistent, significant improvements for both fine-grained and general image classification. These findings support the approach across the tested task types. The broader significance is that useful augmentation depends on preserving the relationship between what an image depicts and what the model is taught about it, as well as producing visually plausible additional examples.
icml-2026-scalda-semantics-calibrated-an.tldr: SCalDA coordinates image, label, and feature semantics during diffusion-enhanced augmentation to improve classification performance.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces numerical precision in an already trained model, but very low bit widths can sharply reduce accuracy. SHARP-Q addresses this by aligning the quantization objective with Fisher information geometry. The approach makes the model's geometric sensitivity central to how quantization is optimized.

Its strategy first rectifies the optimization landscape and then approximates the resulting geometry. Hessian-Aware Rectification performs the preconditioning step. Dynamic Fisher-Subspace Compensation subsequently approximates the rectified Fisher Information Matrix. The order is central to the framework: the geometric approximation operates on a landscape that has already been adjusted, rather than treating these as unrelated corrections.

Experiments span convolutional networks, Vision Transformers, and State Space Models, with substantial accuracy gains in W2A2 and W3A3 settings, where weights and activations both use two or three bits. The authors report new state-of-the-art results and find that geometrically aligned uniform quantizers can outperform specialized non-uniform designs. That empirical finding suggests that improving the optimization geometry can make hardware-friendly quantization competitive even in demanding low-precision regimes.
icml-2026-sharp-q-spectral-hessian-align.tldr: SHARP-Q improves ultra-low-bit post-training quantization by rectifying and approximating the model's Fisher geometry.

paragraphs: Removing visual tokens can reduce computation, but the paper finds that existing reduction methods can severely damage structurally enhanced Mamba models. Its explanation is spatial: these models' selective scanning relies on a two-dimensional arrangement, while conventional reduction may discard the grid and neighborhood relationships that arrangement provides.

STORM makes token reduction explicitly spatial. It operates on structured spatial units and imposes local constraints that preserve grid topology and neighborhood coherence during compression. The framework can be added to existing reduction pipelines without training. Its purpose is to retain the structural assumptions needed by the backbone while still reducing the amount of visual information processed.

Experiments across vision Mamba backbones report state-of-the-art pruning accuracy in training-free settings. On VMamba, the reported improvement over prior methods reaches 63.3% in top-1 accuracy. On PlainMamba, the accuracy drop is only 1.0%, with performance comparable to ViT. These results support the paper's diagnosis that the organization of retained tokens can be crucial to whether compression preserves a visual state space model's performance.
icml-2026-spatial-aware-reduction-framew.tldr: STORM preserves spatial grid and neighborhood structure during training-free token reduction, substantially recovering accuracy in visual Mamba models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates the computation a transformer performs when classifying a new point from labeled examples in its context. It studies multiclass linear classification in a difficult no-margin setting. To make the internal procedure identifiable, the authors enforce feature- and label-permutation equivariance at every layer, so changes in ordering induce corresponding changes in the computation.

These symmetry constraints yield structured weights while maintaining functional equivalence. From the resulting models, the authors extract an explicit recursive update rule indexed by depth. Attention matrices combine feature and label relationships, then drive coupled changes to the training points, their labels, and the test probe. This exposes how successive layers jointly transform the classification problem.

The identified dynamics form a geometry-driven algorithmic pattern that can provably amplify class separation and gives robust expected class alignment. The contribution is an end-to-end account of an emergent update rule inside the studied softmax transformer. Its explanatory force comes from making the computation identifiable under the imposed symmetries within this particular classification setting.
icml-2026-symmetry-reveals-layerwise-dyn.tldr: Layerwise symmetry constraints expose an explicit transformer update rule that can amplify class separation during in-context classification.

paragraphs: Decrypto evaluates how language models reason about other agents during interactive cooperation and competition. Its focus includes theory of mind: reasoning about another participant's mental state. The authors argue that existing evaluations are restricted by issues such as narrow tasks, leakage, saturation, and limited interaction, making multi-agent capabilities difficult to assess.

The benchmark uses a game-based setting informed by cognitive science, computational pragmatics, and multi-agent reinforcement learning. It is designed to keep other demands as easy as possible, reducing factors that could obscure the abilities being tested. The authors evaluate frontier models, study robustness, and run games involving both humans and AI to examine the benchmark's behavior.

Models trail humans and simple word-embedding baselines on key game metrics. The authors also adapt two classic cognitive science experiments to test three distinct theory-of-mind abilities. In those tasks, current reasoning models perform significantly worse than older models. These findings reveal weaknesses in the evaluated interactive reasoning abilities and show why strong performance on other reasoning evaluations need not settle questions about multi-agent competence.
icml-2026-the-decrypto-benchmark-for-mul.tldr: Decrypto tests interactive multi-agent reasoning and finds that leading language models struggle with key game and theory-of-mind tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a shared interpretation of reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization. It views both through mutual-information maximization and connects them to contrastive learning using positive and negative samples derived from a base model. This gives two widely used alignment approaches a common mathematical perspective.

In that interpretation, RLHF and DPO use the Donsker–Varadhan mutual-information lower bound, equivalently the MINE estimator. The perspective also helps explain why RLHF may not intrinsically encourage reasoning capabilities beyond those already present in the base model. This is a qualified claim about the training incentive, rather than a universal assertion that reasoning performance cannot improve.

The authors replace that estimator with a Jensen–Shannon estimator to obtain Mutual Information Optimization, or MIO. Their theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations show that MIO mitigates the late-training decline in the likelihood of preferred responses observed with DPO. It also achieves competitive or better performance across challenging reasoning and mathematics benchmarks, linking the alternative objective to both training behavior and downstream results.
icml-2026-the-hidden-link-between-rlhf-a.tldr: A contrastive-learning interpretation of RLHF and DPO motivates MIO, which mitigates preferred-response likelihood decline and performs competitively on reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper compares reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning in a controlled setting where a one-layer transformer learns sparse Boolean functions through intermediate reasoning steps. The functions considered can be recursively decomposed into fixed two-variable Boolean functions. Reinforcement learning receives verifiable process rewards, making intermediate supervision an explicit part of the comparison.

A unified analysis identifies sufficient conditions under which each training approach provably learns the target function. The authors verify these conditions for k-PARITY, k-AND, and k-OR. These examples establish learnability within the analyzed model and task family; the sufficient conditions describe a route to learning without asserting that it is the only possible route.

The analysis also reveals different learning dynamics. Reinforcement learning learns the full reasoning chain simultaneously, whereas supervised fine-tuning without teacher forcing learns it step by step. This distinction ties the comparison to how intermediate reasoning is supervised. The findings suggest that evaluating RL against SFT should account for that supervision structure, rather than attributing all differences to the broad training-method labels.
icml-2026-transformers-with-rl-or-sft-pr.tldr: Under sufficient conditions, RL and SFT both learn specified sparse Boolean functions, but their intermediate reasoning chains develop differently.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning learns rewards from feedback, reducing the need to manually specify complex objectives. Its practical difficulty is the amount of human labeling required. VOTP addresses this cost in offline learning by combining a small set of preference labels with a much larger collection of unlabeled visual trajectories.

The framework represents those trajectories using a video foundation model and aligns them with optimal transport. This alignment generates high-fidelity pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, extending the supervision available for learning a reward function. The approach is semi-supervised: the human labels provide an initial source of guidance, while visual representations and trajectory matching help carry that guidance across additional data.

Experiments on locomotion and manipulation benchmarks show that VOTP outperforms state-of-the-art offline preference-based methods under limited feedback budgets. The authors also report robustness to visual distractors and demonstrate meaningful reward learning on real robotic tasks with minimal human input. These results support trajectory alignment as a way to reduce labeling demands while retaining useful reward information in the tested settings.
icml-2026-video-based-optimal-transport-.tldr: VOTP uses video representations and optimal transport to generate preference pseudo-labels, improving offline reward learning with limited human feedback.

paragraphs: Preference learning often forces an annotator to choose between two responses even when their quality difference is too small to distinguish. The authors find that such pairs are common in standard benchmarks. A forced choice can then add noise to training, because the recorded preference overstates what the labeler can reliably judge.

The proposed framework allows ties and explicitly incorporates them into optimization. Its objectives seek high-reward regions while reducing unreliable updates that could arbitrarily shift the policy's distribution. The paper also identifies useful tie signals already present in existing benchmarks, allowing these signals to contribute without requiring a new round of labeling.

In the reported experiments, properly modelling ties allows supervision from small models to outperform forced-choice supervision from larger language models or human experts. The proposed approaches also consistently beat the strongest available baselines across the evaluated benchmarks. These findings make a specific case for respecting a labeler's discrimination limit: better use of uncertainty in judgments can outweigh greater labeler capability under the tested forced-choice comparisons.
icml-2026-when-labelers-stay-silent-the-.tldr: Explicitly modelling ties reduces unreliable preference updates and lets small-model supervision outperform stronger forced-choice labelers in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks are usually pretrained for settings where deploying a classifier does not change the data distribution. Strategic behavior breaks that premise: individuals may modify their features to obtain a favorable decision. The paper shows that this creates a mismatch between the pretrained prior and the distribution after manipulation, producing structural prediction bias.

The Strategic Prior-data Fitted Network, or SPN, adapts the model at inference time. It constructs strategic in-context examples that approximate the inputs expected after manipulation, then uses those examples to align predictions with the induced distribution. This requires neither retraining the foundation model nor changing its architecture, and the authors provide theoretical guarantees on bias reduction.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world tabular datasets report consistent improvements in robustness and predictive performance over tabular foundation models and classical tabular methods under strategic manipulation. The contribution is a way to adapt the context supplied to a pretrained predictor so that its assumptions better match behavior caused by deploying the predictor itself.
icml-2026-when-tabular-foundation-models.tldr: SPN uses strategic in-context examples to reduce deployment-induced prediction bias in tabular foundation models without retraining.
